When Plans Change, Remember: Replanning-Guided Visual Memory for Vision-Language-Action Models

Victoria Smelova Affiliation: MIRAI    Daniil Kazachkov Affiliation: MIRAI    Georgiy Kazantsev Affiliation: Independent Researcher    Iuliia Tsvetkova Affiliation: Central University    Egor Cherepanov Affiliation: MIRAI Affiliation: AXXX Affiliation: CogAI LabRePlanMem Website    Nikita Kachaev Affiliation: AXXX Affiliation: CogAI LabRePlanMem Website    Artem Latyshev Affiliation: MIRAI Affiliation: AXXX Affiliation: CogAI LabRePlanMem Website    Aleksandr I. Panov Affiliation: MIRAI Affiliation: CogAI LabRePlanMem Website    Alexey K. Kovalev Affiliation: MIRAI
Abstract

Long-horizon, multi-stage Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies often require visual information that is no longer present in the current observation. Retaining the complete observation history is computationally expensive and highly redundant, motivating selective visual memory. We introduce RePlanMem-VLA (Replanning-Guided Keyframe Memory for VLA), which turns a policy’s own plan revisions into an online memory-write signal. Under receding-horizon execution, consecutive action chunks predict some of the same future actions. RePlanMem-VLA treats unusually large disagreement between these temporally aligned predictions as evidence of a task-relevant event. We first compare 35 disagreement measures across single-task autoregressive decoder-only and Flow-Matching Transformers trained from scratch, then validate the selected signals on pretrained OpenVLA-OFT and π0.5\pi_{0.5} policies over MIKASA-Robo-VLA tasks. The resulting detectors achieve ROC-AUC of 0.981–0.997. We then use the selected signals in RePlanMem-VLA to trigger updates to a bounded visual memory, with a robot-masked write filter suppressing redundant frames. In the evaluated memory-retention experiments, RePlanMem-VLA preserves task-relevant observations until the later decision point in 100%100\% of episodes. Real-robot replay data further show that event selection and redundancy suppression extend beyond simulation. These results establish plan revision as a policy-internal signal for controlling what a VLA remembers. Website: https://vika787.github.io/RePlanMem/.

11footnotetext: These authors contributed equally to this work.

1 Introduction

Long-horizon manipulation often requires Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies to use visual information that has left the current observation, including object properties (Chen et al., 2026a; Shi et al., 2026), earlier environment states (Chen et al., 2026a; Shi et al., 2026), and task progress (Buamanee et al., 2026; Feng et al., 2026). Retaining the full history preserves these cues but increases context length and computation while adding visual redundancy (Jang et al., 2025; Qiu et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026). We therefore seek a small set of informative observations.

We call these observations keyframes: they preserve cues needed later (Shi et al., 2026; Lei et al., 2026) or mark task-phase transitions (Buamanee et al., 2026; Yi et al., 2026). Prior work selects them with vision-language models (Lei et al., 2026), waypoint heuristics (Shi et al., 2023), learned retrieval (Sridhar et al., 2026), progress estimates (Liu et al., 2026), or event detectors (Zeng et al., 2026b). We investigate whether the policy’s own plan revisions can provide an online signal for selecting these observations.

Under receding-horizon execution, consecutive action chunks predict some of the same future actions, while the new plan incorporates the latest observation (Fig. 1). Comparing these temporally aligned predictions reveals how the policy revises its intended behavior after receiving new visual information. Our central hypothesis is that task-relevant observations induce unusually large revisions in predictions for the same future actions. This motivates using plan disagreement as a policy-internal signal to identify candidate keyframes for visual memory.

We introduce RePlanMem-VLA (Replanning-Guided Keyframe Memory for VLA), which derives its selection signal from revisions between overlapping action predictions already produced during normal replanning. Selected keyframes become part of the policy’s visual context, keeping past observations available for subsequent action prediction, while a robot-masked write filter suppresses redundant frames, reducing repeated overwrites. At deployment, the trigger requires neither keyframe annotations nor privileged simulator state.

Our experiments are conducted on MIKASA-Robo-VLA (Cherepanov et al., 2026b), an extension of MIKASA-Robo (Cherepanov et al., 2026a) for evaluating memory-intensive manipulation with VLA policies. We first screen 35 disagreement metrics using autoregressive decoder-only and Flow-Matching Transformers (Lipman et al., 2023) trained from scratch. We then evaluate detectors based on the selected signals with pretrained OpenVLA-OFT (Kim et al., 2025) and π0.5\pi_{0.5} (Physical Intelligence et al., 2025) policies, obtaining ROC-AUC of 0.981–0.997. In the evaluated memory-retention experiments, RePlanMem-VLA preserves task-relevant observations until the later decision point in 100%100\% of episodes, while robot-masked filtering reduces redundant overwrites. Real-robot replay data further support its event-selection and redundancy-suppression behavior beyond simulation (Fig. 2).

Our main contributions are as follows:

  1. 1.

    We introduce RePlanMem-VLA, which identifies keyframes from policy-internal revisions of predictions for the same future actions across consecutive replanning steps (Section 3.3).

  2. 2.

    We identify disagreement measures that best align with keyframe events through systematic analysis across decoder-only and Flow-Matching Transformer policies, and verify their transfer to pretrained OpenVLA-OFT and π0.5\pi_{0.5} policies (Sections 4.1 and 4.2).

  3. 3.

    We develop a bounded visual-memory mechanism where plan disagreement determines when to write and redundancy-aware filtering, including robot-masked clustering, determines what to retain, substantially reducing redundant updates while preserving task-relevant observations (Sections 3 and 4.3).

2 Related Work

Memory for long-horizon, partially observable policies.

Long-horizon manipulation often requires access to information from earlier in the episode. Recent VLA work addresses this through recurrent or belief-state latents (Cherepanov et al., 2026c; Li et al., 2026a), explicit memory representations  (Shi et al., 2026; Guo et al., 2026), long-context or compressed multi-frame conditioning  (Jang et al., 2025), and retrieval- or structure-based memory  (Sridhar et al., 2026; Haresh et al., 2026; Chung et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026b). Memory-dependent manipulation is also studied in dedicated benchmarks  (Cherepanov et al., 2026b; Chen et al., 2026a; Lei et al., 2026). These works study how historical information is represented or retrieved, whereas our focus is on when an observation should be admitted to a bounded memory.

Keyframe and event selection for visual memory.

Existing approaches identify important observations using motion or bottleneck-pose heuristics (James et al., 2022), learned frame scoring (Mark et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026c), progress, value, or critic signals  (Liu et al., 2026; Yi et al., 2026; Buamanee et al., 2026), trajectory annotation (Feng et al., 2026), or dedicated event detectors  (Zeng et al., 2026b) — each relying on a separate selector or external signal. We instead derive the selection signal directly from changes in the acting policy’s own predicted action plans.

Action chunking, replanning, and plan consistency.

Action-chunking policies predict short action sequences and under receding-horizon execution successive chunks overlap on predictions for the same future actions  (Zhao et al., 2023; Chi et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2025; Physical Intelligence et al., 2025). Prior work mainly uses this overlap to improve consistency  (Zhao et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2025) or studies the trade-off between open-loop execution and replanning  (Lazzati et al., 2026; Zeng et al., 2026a; Chen et al., 2026b; Jing et al., 2026). We instead use disagreement between overlapping predictions as a signal that the new observation has changed the policy’s intended behavior.

Memory representation, keyframe selection, and plan consistency are typically studied separately, whereas we connect them by using plan disagreement as a policy-internal signal for memory updates.

3 RePlanMem-VLA

3.1 Overview

In long-horizon manipulation, task-relevant visual information often leaves the cameras before it is needed. A policy that sees only the current frame cannot recover that cue, so we concatenate the live views with a bounded visual memory of BB slots. Slots are empty at the start of an episode and are never carried across episode boundaries. The policy predicts a chunk of KK actions from one observation and executes only the first H<KH<K before replanning, so consecutive chunks overlap on K−HK{-}H future steps: the same intended actions, predicted before and after the new frame. Prior work treats disagreement on that overlap as noise to suppress. We read a large revision as evidence that the new observation was task-relevant and use it to trigger a memory-update proposal. The direct update rule stores the immediately preceding frame, whereas the redundancy-aware variant retains only visual states that are not already represented in memory. Figures 1 and 4 and Algorithm 1 summarize the procedure. At every query the policy first predicts a pre-write chunk from the memory available before a potential write, then overlap disagreement is converted, without gradients, into a task-calibrated surprise score and an event triggers frame selection and a memory update only when a visually novel state is found. The final action prediction is conditioned on the resulting memory state, and only this prediction receives the original supervised fine-tuning (SFT) objective. Event detection never sees expert actions, so memory writes are driven only by the policy’s own plan revisions.

3.2 Memory-augmented action policy

In partially observable manipulation, identical current observations can require different actions depending on earlier cues or task progress (Cherepanov et al., 2026a; Chen et al., 2026a), as illustrated by the delayed-cue setup in Fig. 2. A policy conditioned only on the current observation cannot distinguish such histories. Historical context can resolve this ambiguity, motivating multi-frame conditioning and memory-augmented policies (Jang et al., 2025; Shi et al., 2026). To bound the amount of historical visual input, we retain at most BB observations. The resulting online selection problem is which observations to preserve for future control. We call these observations keyframes, focusing on transient cues needed later and observations marking changes in task phase.

Let qq index policy queries, oqo_{q} denote the current multi-view observation, and ℓ\ell denote the language instruction. Action chunking predicts multiple future controls from a single observation, supporting temporally coordinated behavior and efficient execution (Zhao et al., 2023; Chi et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2025). The policy predicts a chunk of KK actions Cq=(aq,0,…,aq,K−1)C_{q}=(a_{q,0},\ldots,a_{q,K-1}) but executes only the first H<KH<K of them before replanning. We refer to KK and HH as the chunk horizon and execution stride. Here, aq,j∈ℝda_{q,j}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} denotes the action predicted at query qq for the jj-th step of the chunk.

The visual memory before query qq is an ordered collection of at most BB keyframes Mq=(Mq1,…,Mqmq)M_{q}=(M_{q}^{1},\ldots,M_{q}^{m_{q}}), mq≤Bm_{q}\leq B, whose slots are appended to the policy’s visual context alongside the current camera views: with a top and a wrist camera the visual input is Xq=[Iqtop,Iqwrist,Mq1,…,Mqmq]X_{q}=[\,I_{q}^{\mathrm{top}},I_{q}^{\mathrm{wrist}},M_{q}^{1},\ldots,M_{q}^{m_{q}}\,].

All slots are empty at the beginning of an episode, and memory state is never carried across episode boundaries. At query qq, a first forward pass uses the memory state that existed before the current event decision and yields the pre-write plan Cq−=πθ​(oq,Mq,ℓ)C_{q}^{-}=\pi_{\theta}(o_{q},M_{q},\ell), which provides both a candidate control output and the policy-internal signal used to decide whether memory should be updated. We denote the chunk used for execution after the memory-update decision by CqfinalC_{q}^{\mathrm{final}}.

3.3 Plan revision as an event signal

Two consecutive action chunks make predictions for some of the same future time steps. Because HH actions of the preceding chunk have already been executed, the aligned overlap has length K−HK-H. We therefore compare

Uq=Cq−1final[H:K],Vq=Cq−[0:K−H].U_{q}=C_{q-1}^{\mathrm{final}}[H:K],\qquad V_{q}=C_{q}^{-}[0:K-H]. (1)

Both sequences estimate the same future actions, but VqV_{q} is conditioned on the newly observed scene, so a large discrepancy indicates that new visual evidence has caused the policy to revise its intended behavior. We summarize this revision with DD complementary detector signals 𝒚q=[yq1,…,yqD]⊤\bm{y}_{q}=[y_{q}^{1},\ldots,y_{q}^{D}]^{\top}. These signals include aligned action error, directional disagreement, temporally localized deviations, translation, rotation, and gripper changes. The deployed detector also includes the distance between consecutive detached top-view VLA features as one of these signals. In our configuration D=10D=10.

To distinguish persistent model uncertainty from abrupt changes, we augment these values with their temporal differences Δ​𝒚q=𝒚q−𝒚q−1\Delta\bm{y}_{q}=\bm{y}_{q}-\bm{y}_{q-1} and with causal deviations from an exponential moving average (EMA),

𝒎~q=β​𝒎~q−1+(1−β)​𝒚q,𝒅q,EMA=𝒚q−𝒎~q−1.\widetilde{\bm{m}}_{q}=\beta\widetilde{\bm{m}}_{q-1}+(1-\beta)\bm{y}_{q},\qquad\bm{d}_{q,\mathrm{EMA}}=\bm{y}_{q}-\widetilde{\bm{m}}_{q-1}.

The complete detector input is

𝒙q=[𝒚q⊤,Δ​𝒚q⊤,𝒅q,EMA⊤]⊤∈ℝ3​D,\bm{x}_{q}=\left[\bm{y}_{q}^{\top},\Delta\bm{y}_{q}^{\top},\bm{d}_{q,\mathrm{EMA}}^{\top}\right]^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{3D}, (2)

which is ℝ30\mathbb{R}^{30} in our configuration. All quantities entering Eqs. (1) and (2) are computed from stop-gradient copies of action chunks and visual features. Consequently, the event detector cannot shape the policy by differentiating through its decision rule.

3.4 Causal, task-conditioned event detection

The components of 𝒙q\bm{x}_{q} have different units and dynamic ranges, so we standardize each of them using statistics available strictly before the current query, zqi=(xqi−μq−1i,(k))/(σq−1i,(k)+ε)z_{q}^{i}=(x_{q}^{i}-\mu_{q-1}^{i,(k)})/(\sigma_{q-1}^{i,(k)}+\varepsilon). The current sample is scored before it is incorporated into the running statistics. All detector statistics — the moments, the matrix below, and the reference cumulative distribution function (CDF) of Eq. (4) — are maintained separately for each task kk, so that no cross-task scale difference enters the score. Let 𝚺q−1(k)\bm{\Sigma}_{q-1}^{(k)} be the causal second-moment matrix of the normalized features. Because the preceding normalization is component-wise, its diagonal is unity up to the lag of the running moments, so 𝚺q−1(k)\bm{\Sigma}_{q-1}^{(k)} acts as a correlation matrix. The joint deviation of the features is measured by the regularized Mahalanobis surprise:

Sq=𝒛q⊤​(𝚺q−1(k)+λ​𝑰)−1​𝒛q,S_{q}=\sqrt{\bm{z}_{q}^{\top}\left(\bm{\Sigma}_{q-1}^{(k)}+\lambda\bm{I}\right)^{-1}\bm{z}_{q}}, (3)

where λ>0\lambda>0 stabilizes the inversion. We set it to a fixed fraction of the mean eigenvalue of 𝚺q−1(k)\bm{\Sigma}_{q-1}^{(k)}, which makes the regularizer scale-free across tasks. Unlike an unweighted Euclidean norm, Eq. (3) accounts for correlations among different revision signals.

Natural plan variability differs across tasks in multi-task SFT, which is why the calibration above is per-task while the decision threshold is shared. Writing Fk​(s)=Pr⁡(S≤s∣k)F_{k}(s)=\Pr(S\leq s\mid k) for the empirical CDF of past surprise scores for task kk, the event percentile and binary decision are

pq=Fk(Sq),eq=[pq>τ].p_{q}=F_{k}(S_{q}),\qquad e_{q}=\mathbf{1}\!\left[p_{q}>\tau\right]. (4)

Thus τ=0.99\tau=0.99, for example, assigns the same interpretation — an event more surprising than 99%99\% of the task-specific reference distribution — across heterogeneous tasks. At the beginning of SFT, memory writes are disabled for a short warm-up period (the first 55–10%10\% of training), while the policy is optimized normally and detector statistics are collected. After warm-up, the CDFs and causal moments can be updated with rolling histories to track the changing policy. Once training is complete, these statistics are frozen and kept fixed at inference time to preserve a stable detector calibration. The first query in each episode has no preceding chunk and cannot produce a plan-overlap event.

3.5 Redundancy-aware frame selection

An event determines when memory should be reconsidered, but not necessarily which frame should be stored. At an event, we jointly consider the current FIFO contents and a short causal window WqW_{q} of observations preceding the current query. We use the three observations preceding the event query (W=3W=3) and apply deterministic complete-link clustering with threshold δ=0.01\delta=0.01. From each novel cluster, the most recent candidate is selected as its representative. The current observation is excluded so that selection cannot use information obtained after the detected plan revision.

We group visually similar frames using complete-link clustering and treat a candidate cluster as novel only if it contains no frame already represented in memory. From each novel cluster, we retain its most recent candidate and append the selected representatives to the bounded FIFO in chronological order. Thus, one detector event may result in zero, one, or multiple writes. Visual masks, when available, are used only to suppress irrelevant appearance changes during comparison, while the original RGB frames are stored and supplied to the policy. The direct update rule is the special case in which the selector returns only the immediately preceding frame without redundancy filtering.

3.6 Event-gated memory update and second forward pass

When an event is detected at query qq, the frame-selection rule returns a possibly empty sequence RqR_{q} of candidate keyframes. The direct rule returns the immediately preceding top-view observation, whereas the redundancy-aware rule may return zero, one, or multiple frames. A fixed-capacity FIFO operator produces

Mq+=FIFOAppend⁡(Mq,Rq),M_{q}^{+}=\operatorname{FIFOAppend}(M_{q},R_{q}),

inserting the selected frames in chronological order and discarding the oldest items when all BB slots are occupied. If Rq=∅R_{q}=\varnothing, memory remains unchanged even though the detector emitted an event.

At inference time, an actual memory update is followed by a second evaluation of the same policy on the current observation and instruction,

Cqfinal=πθ​(oq,Mq+,ℓ).C_{q}^{\mathrm{final}}=\pi_{\theta}(o_{q},M_{q}^{+},\ell).

If no frame is written, no additional inference pass is required and Cqfinal=Cq−C_{q}^{\mathrm{final}}=C_{q}^{-}. During distributed SFT, the inference-only pre-write pass is followed by one differentiable final pass for the complete micro-batch, so rows without a memory update simply use the unchanged memory state. This keeps the distributed computation graph synchronized when event counts differ across ranks.

3.7 Supervised fine-tuning objective

Let AqGTA_{q}^{\mathrm{GT}} be the expert action chunk associated with query qq. We retain the backbone’s standard action objective and apply it only to the selected final chunk, ℒSFT​(θ)=∑qℒact​(Cqfinal,AqGT)\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SFT}}(\theta)=\sum_{q}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{act}}(C_{q}^{\mathrm{final}},A_{q}^{\mathrm{GT}}). Gradients flow through the policy invocation that produced CqfinalC_{q}^{\mathrm{final}}, but not through the detector, its running statistics, or the discrete memory-write decision. Expert actions supervise control only: they are not used to identify events or select keyframes. The same causal detector and memory-update procedure can therefore be used at inference time without keyframe annotations or privileged simulator state.

4 Experimental evaluation

Our experiments address three Research Questions (RQs):

  1. RQ1.

    Does revision of overlapping action chunks contain a task-relevant signal, and which disagreement measures extract it most reliably?

  2. RQ2.

    Does this signal transfer to pretrained VLA policies across different backbones and replanning frequencies, and can it support accurate online event detection?

  3. RQ3.

    Can the resulting surprise signal be used to drive selective visual-memory updates during VLA fine-tuning?

4.1 RQ1: Disagreement signals in single-task policies

We first examine whether disagreement between overlapping action predictions contains task-relevant information using single-task autoregressive and Flow-Matching Transformers trained from scratch. This analysis allows us to efficiently screen a large set of disagreement metrics at substantially lower computational cost before transferring the most informative signals to pretrained VLA policies. We evaluate 35 disagreement metrics (Appendix C) across eight MIKASA-Robo-VLA tasks (Appendix A.1) and examine whether their behavior remains consistent across different task structures and amounts of available historical information. For each architecture, we compare two regimes: full-context, where the policy has access to the full observation history up to the current query, and current-only, where the prediction is conditioned only on the current observation.

Visual analysis of disagreement profiles shows that scores often remain near a relatively stable baseline, with peaks occurring near keyframes. This pattern motivates a simple threshold-based rule: a frame is predicted as a keyframe when its disagreement score exceeds a threshold. We use Frame ROC-AUC as the primary screening criterion, evaluating how well these predictions match reference keyframe labels across detection thresholds. A more detailed analysis, including correlation analysis, and task-specific results, is provided in Appendix A.

Experiments show that disagreement measures remain informative both with and without observation history, although their effectiveness varies across tasks and settings. On tasks with clear phase transitions, such as RememberColor3-VLA-v0 and ShellGameColorLampTouch-VLA-v0, for autoregressive policies, Causal Z-score reaches Frame ROC-AUC of 0.798/0.7460.798/0.746 under full-context/current-only conditioning, with EMA deviation showing a similar pattern (0.790/0.7120.790/0.712). For Flow-Matching policies, distributional measures achieve higher scores: Wasserstein-1 reaches 0.93880.9388 and Energy distance 0.94270.9427. Translation, rotation, and gripper disagreement also perform well, with scores ranging from 0.8510.851 to 0.9110.911. Causal Z-score remains stable (0.696/0.6900.696/0.690), showing that the causal temporal signal persists across both action-generation paradigms.

The broader analysis establishes disagreement between consecutive action chunks as a useful signal of keyframes, with several types of plan revision measures contributing useful information across tasks. These signals remain informative across action-generation architectures and context regimes and remain visible on failed trajectories (Appendix A.3). Correlation analysis further reveals substantial redundancy within metric families (Appendix A.4), indicating that closely related measures often provide similar information about plan-revision structure. These findings motivate selecting a compact set of complementary disagreement features for the subsequent VLA experiments.

4.2 RQ2: Event detection with pretrained VLA policies

We next evaluate whether a compact combination of metrics remains effective for online event detection in pretrained VLA policies across different backbones and replanning frequencies. Building on RQ1, we select nine representative metrics spanning the distributional, cumulative, and causal temporal signals and augment them with a VLA-specific visual feature that captures changes in the policy’s visual representation between consecutive observations. The resulting ten features (Table 1) serve as input to learned keyframe detectors.

We evaluate pretrained OpenVLA-OFT (Kim et al., 2025) and π0.5\pi_{0.5} (Physical Intelligence et al., 2025) policies on 19 MIKASA-Robo-VLA tasks, under two execution regimes: replanning after every action (RH1, H=1H=1) and executing four actions before replanning (EXEC4, H=4H=4). Both policies predict chunks of K=8K=8 actions. For each pair of consecutive plans, we compute the selected metrics over their temporally aligned overlap. Together with the visual-change feature, these measurements provide the input for three types of keyframe detectors: XGBoost (Chen and Guestrin, 2016), CatBoost (Prokhorenkova et al., 2018), and a causal LSTM (Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, 1997). The detectors are trained using simulator phase transitions as reference keyframe labels.

For detection evaluation we use ROC-AUC and PR-AUC. As in RQ1, ROC-AUC measures how well detector scores separate keyframes from other observations across thresholds. PR-AUC evaluates the trade-off between precision and recall, reflecting whether the detectors identify keyframes while limiting false detections. Table 2 shows that both metrics remain high across policies, execution regimes, and detector types: ROC-AUC ranges from 0.9810.981 to 0.9970.997, and PR-AUC from 0.9240.924 to 0.9960.996. The causal LSTM, which also incorporates information from preceding queries, achieves the highest PR-AUC under RH1 for both OpenVLA-OFT (0.9620.962) and π0.5\pi_{0.5} (0.9330.933). Detection remains strong under EXEC4, where XGBoost achieves the highest PR-AUC for OpenVLA-OFT (0.9960.996), while the LSTM performs best for π0.5\pi_{0.5} (0.9830.983).

We additionally evaluate event​_​recall​@​1\mathrm{event\_recall@1}, which measures whether each reference event has at least one detection within a ±1\pm 1-step window around its phase boundary. All three detectors achieve event​_​recall​@​1=1.0\mathrm{event\_recall@1}=1.0, showing that every reference event is detected within this window. Together, these results support using the selected features for online keyframe detection and motivate their use for visual-memory updates in RePlanMem-VLA. The experimental protocol and extended results are provided in Appendix B.

4.3 RQ3: Surprise-gated visual-memory updates

We finally investigate whether plan disagreement can guide visual-memory updates in tasks that require information from earlier observations. Specifically, taking the RememberColor task as an example, we examine whether the selected observations are written and remain available in memory until they are needed for action selection.

4.3.1 Direct surprise-gated writing

We first evaluate the simplest memory-update rule, in which each detected event directly writes the immediately preceding top-view observation to the FIFO. We examine the resulting memory-write behavior using π0.5\pi_{0.5} and OpenVLA-OFT on RememberColor3-VLA-v0, testing different detector thresholds for writing keyframes to memory. At the 95th-percentile threshold, the cue observation is written in fewer than 20%20\% of the evaluated π0.5\pi_{0.5} episodes and in none of the evaluated OpenVLA-OFT episodes, whereas the runs with an 80th-percentile threshold achieve cue-writing rates of 48%48\% and 85%85\%, respectively. Disagreement peaks also often span several replanning steps, leading to repeated writes of observations associated with the same keyframe event (Fig. 3). These observations motivate using a lower detection threshold and selecting visually distinct frames rather than writing an observation at every query above the threshold.

4.3.2 Redundancy-aware memory selection

We next replace direct writes with the redundancy-aware selector from Section 3.5. At each detected event, we examine a short window of preceding observations and group visually similar frames together with the observations already stored in memory. We then select the most recent frame from each group not represented in memory. This allows the selector to identify candidate keyframes associated with the detected plan revision while avoiding repeated writes of visually similar observations.

With the addition of clustering, cue-writing and retention rates for OpenVLA-OFT improve to 100%100\% in the evaluated 50 episodes. However, observations of the same environment state can still be assigned to different clusters because of changes in robot pose, leading to frequent memory overwrites. With a bounded FIFO memory, these redundant writes can evict task-relevant information observed during the early stages of the episode. This motivates masking the robot during visual comparison to suppress redundant updates caused by manipulator motion.

4.3.3 Robot-masked redundancy filtering

We next add robot masking to the frame-selection procedure and evaluate its effect on memory updates. The masks shown in Figure 5 are applied only during visual comparison, while the original RGB observations are stored in memory and supplied to the VLA. For OpenVLA-OFT, across 50 evaluated episodes, robot masking nearly halves the number of memory writes from 336 to 169 and reduces FIFO evictions by almost a factor of ten, from 186 to 19. At the same time, the task-relevant keyframe is written and retained until the action phase in all 50/5050/50 episodes.

We thus obtain a mechanism that uses plan disagreement to successfully detect keyframes and retain them in visual memory.

4.3.4 Transfer to real-robot replay

Finally, we evaluate the same event-detection and redundancy-filtering pipeline through offline replay of recorded real-robot trajectories, testing the event detector, visual clustering, and robot-masked similarity outside simulation.

Figure 6 illustrates how the detector responds to keyframes associated with phase transitions in the RememberColor task, while robot masking suppresses redundant memory overwrites during the action phase.

5 Limitations and Future Work

Our experiments show that disagreement between overlapping action chunks can accurately identify task-relevant keyframes. However, we do not claim that such disagreement is specific to semantic events. Substantial plan revisions may also arise for other reasons, including policy prediction errors. The proposed signal should therefore be interpreted as an indicator of potentially important change rather than as an unambiguous semantic event detector.

Another limitation concerns the temporal structure of the evaluated tasks. The task phases in our experiments have relatively clear boundaries. With an execution stride of H=4H=4, short phases may occur entirely between two replanning queries and therefore be missed, whereas gradual transitions may distribute the corresponding plan revision over several queries and produce no pronounced peak. How disagreement behaves under less distinct phase transitions remains to be investigated.

Our current implementation stores selected observations as full images in a small visual memory and uses visual clustering to suppress redundant entries. A promising direction is therefore to develop more compact representations of stored observations, together with comparison and aggregation mechanisms that preserve task-relevant information while making historical context easier for the policy to use.

Finally, the current surprise estimate is defined relative to task-conditioned statistics accumulated from previous replanning queries, and the write threshold is selected empirically. Consequently, the present formulation requires calibration data for each task and has not yet been shown to transfer directly to previously unseen tasks without accumulating new reference statistics and selecting an appropriate threshold.

6 Conclusion

We investigated whether revisions of overlapping action chunks can serve as an internal signal of observation importance in long-horizon robot control. Across single-task autoregressive and Flow-Matching policies, we find that disagreement between consecutive plans contains a consistent signal of semantic task transitions, with complementary distributional, cumulative, and causal temporal measures capturing different aspects of plan revision. We further show that this signal transfers to pretrained OpenVLA-OFT and π0.5\pi_{0.5} policies across different replanning frequencies and remains predictive even when control performance varies substantially. Building on these observations, we use disagreement-derived surprise to drive selective visual-memory updates in a memory-augmented VLA policy. The resulting framework connects three stages that are usually treated separately: replanning, event detection, and memory formation. Rather than introducing an external keyframe selector, the policy reuses a signal that naturally arises from its own action predictions to decide when the observation history should be updated. Overall, our results suggest that changes in a policy’s intended future behavior provide a useful source of temporal proposals for sparse memory updates in partially observable, multi-stage manipulation.

Appendix A Additional Analysis for RQ1

This appendix details the experimental setup, evaluation protocol, and supporting analyses for Section 4.1.

A.1 Experimental setup and reference events

Tasks and training.

The single-task screening uses eight MIKASA-Robo-VLA tasks (Cherepanov et al., 2026b): RememberColor3-VLA-v0, ShellGameColorLampTouch-VLA-v0, ShellGameShuffleColorLampTouch-VLA-v0, ShellGameShuffleTouch-VLA-v0, FindImposterShape3-VLA-v0, InterceptSlow-VLA-v0, RotateLenientPos-VLA-v0, and TakeItBack-VLA-v0. Each policy is trained from scratch on 250 demonstrations of a single task. A separate policy is trained for each combination of task, architecture, and context regime for 150 epochs, using training seed 42.

Observations and policy architectures.

Each observation contains top-view and wrist-camera RGB images at 128×128128\times 128 resolution and a seven-dimensional proprioceptive state describing the end-effector pose and gripper position. The images are scaled to [0,1][0,1], concatenated along the channel dimension, and encoded by NatureCNN. Proprioception and action targets are standardized using training-set statistics. For RotateLenientPos-VLA-v0, the policy additionally receives the numerical target angle from the task instruction.

Both architectures use the same visual and proprioceptive encoder configurations and context Transformer settings. Their shared settings and architecture-specific components are summarized in Table 3.

Execution and evaluation.

Both architectures predict action chunks of length K=8K=8 and execute one action before replanning (H=1H=1). During Flow-Matching evaluation, a fixed Gaussian noise tensor is reused across queries within each rollout to prevent stochastic resampling from introducing artificial plan disagreement. For each task and context regime, each policy is evaluated on 50 closed-loop episodes.

Reference keyframes.

Task-specific simulator events provide the reference keyframe labels. For a phase transition between observations b−1b-1 and bb, we define the reference event window as

ℐe=[b−1,b].\mathcal{I}_{e}=[b-1,b].

Both the final observation of the preceding phase and the first observation of the following phase are labelled as keyframes. All remaining observations are labelled as non-keyframes. The task-specific reference events are listed in Table 5.

A.2 Task-specific results

Table 4 reports the best-performing disagreement metric and its Frame ROC-AUC for each task, architecture, and context regime.

A.3 Disagreement signals on failed trajectories

Execution and evaluation.

We examine whether disagreement remains informative when the policy fails to complete the task. Frame ROC-AUC is computed separately for successful and failed trajectories within each task and summarized by the median across tasks.

For autoregressive policies, median Causal Z-score ROC-AUC on failed trajectories is 0.700/0.6910.700/0.691 under full-context/current-only conditioning, compared with 0.589/0.5380.589/0.538 on successful trajectories. For Flow-Matching policies, Wasserstein-1 reaches 0.732/0.7410.732/0.741 on failed trajectories, compared with 0.670/0.6400.670/0.640 on successful trajectories. The direction of the difference depends on the measure, with Flow-Matching EMA deviation performing better on successful trajectories. Overall, task failure does not lead to a systematic decrease in disagreement-based keyframe discrimination.

A.4 Correlation structure and metric redundancy

We assess whether different disagreement measures provide similar information by computing pairwise Spearman correlations between their within-episode score sequences. Correlations are summarized within each task and aggregated with equal weight across the eight tasks. Figure 7 shows the resulting matrices for both architectures and context regimes.

The matrices reveal substantial redundancy among magnitude-based measures, including several point-wise, cumulative, and distributional metrics. Causal Z-score and EMA deviation are less strongly correlated with many of these measures, suggesting that their temporal normalization captures a different aspect of plan revision.

The overall correlation structure remains similar across context regimes. Spearman correlations between the corresponding off-diagonal entries of the full-context and current-only matrices are 0.96470.9647 for autoregressive policies and 0.97420.9742 for Flow-Matching policies. These analyses motivate using a compact feature set rather than retaining many closely correlated variants.

Appendix B Additional Analysis for RQ2

This appendix details the experimental protocol and extended results for Section 4.2.

B.1 Experimental setup and evaluation

Tasks and policy fine-tuning.

Both OpenVLA-OFT and π0.5\pi_{0.5} are fine-tuned on the same 19 MIKASA-Robo-VLA tasks (Cherepanov et al., 2026b): FindImposterColor3-VLA-v0, FindImposterColor5-VLA-v0, FindImposterColor9-VLA-v0, FindImposterShape3-VLA-v0, FindImposterShape5-VLA-v0, FindImposterShape9-VLA-v0, FindImposterShapeAndColor3x2-VLA-v0, FindImposterShapeAndColor3x3-VLA-v0, FindImposterShapeAndColor5x3-VLA-v0, RememberColor3-VLA-v0, RememberColor5-VLA-v0, RememberColor9-VLA-v0, RememberShape3-VLA-v0, RememberShape5-VLA-v0, RememberShape9-VLA-v0, RememberShapeAndColor3x2-VLA-v0, RememberShapeAndColor3x3-VLA-v0, RememberShapeAndColor5x3-VLA-v0, and TakeItBack-VLA-v0.

Detector training and evaluation.

To train and evaluate the keyframe detectors, we collect 50 closed-loop episodes for each task, policy, and execution regime. The resulting trajectories are divided at the episode level into approximately 70% training, 10% validation, and 20% test subsets, keeping each episode intact and preserving the temporal order of its observations. Detectors are trained independently for each policy and execution regime, with decision thresholds selected by maximizing F1 on the validation episodes.

B.2 Within-episode detection profiles

Figure 8 shows selected disagreement features and detector outputs during RememberColor5 episodes for both policies under RH1 and EXEC4.
